paragraphs.text: The shopping is done, the fire is lit, and the language turns friendly. Three photographs show three moments at the table: the first bite, the second helping offered, the refusal offered politely. Each one is only two or three lines long — read them aloud before you listen, and the audio will feel slow.

Look at how a no is built here. Nobody simply says {{de:nein}} and stops; the refusal comes with thanks and a reason: {{de:Nein, danke. Ich bin satt}} or {{de:Nein, danke. Ich esse keine Gurken}}. The reason is the manners. Keep the pattern whole and you can decline food without disappointing the cook.
Guten Appetit! — Danke, gleichfalls! · Schmeckt's? — Mmh, ja, das Fleisch schmeckt sehr gut!

paragraphs.text: {{de:möchten}} is the polite way to say you want something. Where {{de:wollen}} states a decision, {{de:möchten}} asks — which is why every offer on this page is built with it. It behaves like a verb you already know: one ending for {{de:du}}, one for the third person, and nothing new for the rest.
ich möchte · du möchtest · er/es/sie möchte · wir möchten · ihr möchtet · sie/Sie möchten

Notice the endings {{de:-st}} on {{de:du}} and {{de:-t}} on {{de:ihr}} — the same two endings you met in the present tense of regular verbs. Only the singular forms carry an umlaut; the plural stays plain {{de:möchten}}.
